Modern.tagline: A podcast network for people who like a clear point of view.
Modern.brandNameRationale: Outloud is a compound word — out + loud — that names what podcasts do: they speak ideas out loud, with a person attached. The compound feels modern and slightly punchy without being literal about audio. Stands in the lineage of single-word podcast network names (Wondery, Crooked, Gimlet, Pushkin) — short, evocative, easy to print on a sticker, no audio-vocabulary cliché.
Modern.manifesto: Most podcast networks try to be a library — three hundred shows, every genre, an algorithm. We made Outloud because the network worth listening to is the small one — twelve shows, all with a point of view, hosts who would argue with each other if you put them in a room. The network is curated, not catalogued. The shows are picked the way a small bookshop picks its front table.
Modern.industrySummary: Podcast networks have split between the broad platforms (Spotify, iHeart) and the narrow editorial networks (Pushkin, Crooked, Defector). The opening underneath is for a smaller editorial network with a clear curatorial point of view and a small show roster.
Modern.competitorLandscape: Pushkin Industries (pushkin.fm) holds the prestige editorial network slot. Crooked Media (crooked.com) plays in the political-editorial peer position. Defector (defector.com) sits in the journalist-owned middle. Radiotopia (radiotopia.fm) is the public-radio peer reference. We sit alongside Pushkin and Radiotopia with a tighter editorial focus.
Modern.positioningStatement: Outloud is a curated editorial podcast network of twelve shows, picked for point of view, not for genre.
Modern.positioningRationale: We compete on curation discipline. Twelve shows on the network at a time. New shows are added rarely; existing shows are renewed annually based on the network's editorial fit, not download numbers.

Luxury.brandNameRationale: Atticus is a name. It comes from antiquity and shows up again in literature. The word carries seriousness and a slight literary register. Naming a podcast network after a person, not a thing, makes it sound like the curator's voice is the brand.
Luxury.story: Atticus began with three founders who had spent a decade inside large media companies. They wanted to produce a small number of shows, very well, and listen to themselves more. The network has stayed at twelve shows since the beginning.
Luxury.industrySummary: Premium podcasts have been moving toward big-name guests and high production budgets. There's a smaller market for the literary side. Long form, narrative, considered, hosted by people who would have been magazine writers in another era.
Luxury.competitorLandscape: Pushkin Industries (pushkin.fm) is the closest in literary register. Audible Originals (audible.com) holds the prestige-talent side. The New Yorker Radio Hour (newyorker.com/podcasts) does it under another brand. We sit in the same room as Pushkin, with fewer shows.

Luxury.brandNameRationale: Lyceum is the ancient Greek school where Aristotle taught — the original setting for the long-form intellectual lecture. As a brand name it places the work firmly in the knowledge-tradition register. Audio is the plain category suffix. The pair reads as a serious audio house — closer to a publisher than to a network — in the lineage of small premium audio brands (Pushkin Industries in tone, Slate Plus Original Lectures, BBC Reith Lectures register).
Luxury.story: Lyceum Audio is a small audio publisher producing six long-form lecture series a year. Each series is twelve to twenty episodes, eighty minutes per episode, recorded with a single speaker in a treated room. Speakers are scholars, writers, and senior practitioners — never celebrities. Series are sold individually, not through subscription.
Luxury.industrySummary: Premium podcasting has been claimed by celebrity-host networks (Pushkin's Malcolm Gladwell shows, SmartLess, Conan O'Brien) but the long-form lecture tradition — the BBC Reith Lectures, the Massey Lectures, university-press audio — remains underserved as a commercial format. There is space for a small audio publisher producing long-form lectures from serious speakers.
Luxury.competitorLandscape: Pushkin Industries (pushkin.fm) is the prestige peer reference. The Great Courses (thegreatcourses.com) holds the lecture-format reference. BBC Sounds (bbc.co.uk/sounds) sits in the public-broadcaster peer position. Audible Originals (audible.com/originals) plays in the platform-publisher slot. We sit further out — six series a year, sold individually.
Luxury.positioningStatement: Lyceum Audio publishes six long-form lecture series per year, each from a single serious speaker, sold individually.
Luxury.positioningRationale: We do not run a subscription. We do not run a network. Each series is a discrete published work, like a book — researched, recorded, mastered, and released with a printed companion volume.

Minimal.positioningStatement: A podcast network for the listener who only wants the audio.

Minimal.brandNameRationale: Volume is a real audio-vocabulary word — the magnitude of sound — and also the publishing word for a single book in a series. The double meaning is useful: the brand is both audio and published work. Single-word, archaic in everyday speech, immediately readable in context. Stands in the lineage of single-word minimal media brands (Quiet, The Slate, Editorial) without being literal.
Minimal.manifesto: Most podcasts pad. Three-minute pre-rolls, four-minute promos, six-minute intros explaining the format. We made Volume because the actual interesting thing is the conversation. We open the episode with the conversation. We close when the conversation ends. There is no ad break, no host welcome, no merchandise pitch. The whole episode is the volume.
Minimal.industrySummary: Most podcast hosting has accumulated production conventions — pre-roll, mid-roll, sponsor reads, host banter, format intros. There is real space for a minimal show that strips the format and trusts the content to do the work.
Minimal.competitorLandscape: Conversations with Tyler (conversationswithtyler.com) plays in the unedited-conversation peer space. The Tim Ferriss Show (tim.blog/podcast) holds the long-conversation reference with edits. EconTalk (econtalk.org) sits in the academic-conversation slot. We sit further out — fewer cuts, no intro, no outro.
Minimal.positioningStatement: Volume is an interview podcast that opens with the conversation and ends when it ends.

Creative.tagline: Shows you'd overhear in a good bar.
Creative.brandNameRationale: Earshot is a real word for the distance within which a conversation can be heard — slightly literary, slightly intimate, immediately evocative of the eavesdropping pleasure good podcasts deliver. Podcast Co. is the plain category suffix. The pair reads as a small, warm production house with a clear point of view — closer in tone to Radiotopia or Pineapple Street than to a corporate network.
Creative.manifesto: Most podcast networks chase scale. More shows, more genres, more downloads. We started Earshot because the actually good podcasts feel like overhearing a great conversation in a bar — specific, unhurried, with a clear point of view from a host you start to like. The network is small. The shows are warm. The conversations stay specific.
Creative.industrySummary: Editorial podcast networks have proliferated. The opening is for a network with a tonal point of view — warm, conversational, slightly bar-room — that differentiates from both the polished prestige networks (Pushkin) and the genre-driven entertainment networks (Wondery).
Creative.competitorLandscape: Radiotopia (radiotopia.fm) holds the indie-editorial peer slot. Pineapple Street Studios (pineapple.fm) plays in the warm-editorial middle. Defector (defector.com) sits in the journalist-owned peer position. The Ringer (theringer.com) is the conversational-network reference. We sit alongside Radiotopia with a stronger tonal identity.
Creative.positioningStatement: Earshot Podcast Co. is a small editorial network producing warm, conversational shows with clear hosts and unhurried pacing.
Creative.positioningRationale: The network competes on tone. Every show on the roster is selected for warmth, specificity, and host personality — not for category fit or download projections.

targetAudience.primary: Listeners 28–50 who follow specific hosts and value tone over genre.
behaviors: Subscribe to under ten podcasts.
Listen at 1x, sometimes 1.25x.
Follow hosts on social media as friends.
Recommend shows to specific people, not generally.
motivations: Want shows that feel like a friend's recommendation.
Want hosts they can imagine having a drink with.

dos: Lead with the host's voice and a sample line from a recent episode.
Photograph the hosts in real places, not in studios.
Write show descriptions in the host's voice.
Publish a weekly handpicked-episodes letter.

messagingPillars.name: Hosts as the brand
messagingPillars.description: Each host's social presence, newsletter, and live events sit under the network umbrella. The hosts are the marketing channel.

messagingPillars.name: Weekly letter
messagingPillars.description: One letter a week, written by the network editor, recommending three episodes from across the network with a sentence each.
